opening.headline: Learn exactly what the word "agent" means, and the criteria for judging when to use an agent and when not to use it.
body: The word “agent” is used differently for each product. Chat tools, code editing tools, and automation scripts are all called agents. If the name is the same, it is easy to think that the structure is the same, but in reality, the costs and risks are significantly different.

In this lesson, we distinguish between the definitions of workflow and agents, and look at the process of one cycle of the agent loop. Next, we compare ReAct and planned agents, analyze the path through which costs increase when using agents for fixed procedure tasks, and distinguish cases when they should not be used. We also look at the role models and apps play in tool calls, context windows and tokens, and how errors accumulate.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the difference between workflow and agent
You can distinguish cases when you should not use an agent.
Distinguish between the roles of models and apps in tool calls, and explain how context windows and error accumulation impact cost and trust.

screens.title: Should all automation have agents?
screens.lead: First, read what one team went through. I read this while thinking about where the decision to introduce agents went wrong.

visual.alt: A scene where two tasks from the same team are drawn with different paths.
labels: Order inquiry → Stock check → Template email sent
The procedure is always the same
You don't know in advance what you will see
Increased response time, multiple times token cost

paragraphs: One team said, “Everything is an agent these days,” and introduced agents to automate the sending of order confirmation emails. The procedure for this automation was originally fixed. It was three steps: track the order, check inventory, and send an email based on the template.

After introduction, the response time per call increased, and the monthly token cost multiplied several times. Sometimes we even call tools that we don't need. Code modification tasks undertaken by the same team are just the opposite. Since demands are different every time, fixed procedures cannot be used to respond.

Trying to apply the same tool to both tasks increases costs on one side and lacks flexibility on the other side. This lesson answers three questions: What is an agent, when should I use it, and when should I not use it?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Order confirmation emails and login bug fixes are both subject to automation. What differences between the two tasks require different structures?

screens.outro: Let me first think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: What comes to mind when you hear the word “agent”?
items.answer: Each person has a different image. Chatbots that speak to you, tools that fix code, and schedule automation are all called agents. Because the same word is used differently for each product, this class first accurately defines the terminology.

items.prompt: How have you differentiated between tasks that can be completed through a single chat and tasks that require using tools multiple times?
items.answer: There is a difference between a job that ends with a single question and answer and a job that requires looking at intermediate results to decide the next action. The former task requires a single call, while the latter task requires a structure where the model looks at the results and chooses the next step.

items.prompt: Have you ever had an experience where automation was more complicated than necessary and difficult to manage?
items.answer: The more powerful a tool is, the more likely we are to spend more than we need to. However, complex structures also bring costs, delays, and debugging burdens. That's why you need to start with the simplest solution.

screens.outro: First, let's distinguish between workflow and agent and look at the structure of the agent loop.

screens.title: How tool calls work: the model makes a request and the app executes
screens.lead: If you select the number marker in the picture, you can see step by step the process of one tool call. Try pressing markers 1 to 4 in order.

visual.alt: A round-trip structure diagram in which tool definition, call request, execution, and results are exchanged between the app code and model.
labels: Tool implementation: reading files, executing commands, calling APIs
Tool definition: name, description, input schema
Call request: call ID, tool name, input values
Result: Added to conversation with call ID
Just make a request and don't execute it

markers.label: tool definition
markers.title: The app will tell you which tools you can use first
markers.body: The app passes the model a list of tools it can use with each request. Each definition contains the tool name, a sentence describing what the tool does, and an input schema that specifies the format of the input values. The model picks a tool based solely on its definition, without seeing the tool's implementation code. Ambiguity in the description can lead to choosing the wrong tool or filling out input values ​​incorrectly, so the definition is an instruction manual that the model reads.

markers.label: call request
markers.title: Model writes structured requests
markers.body: When the model determines that a tool is needed, the response contains a structured call request instead of a regular sentence. The request contains an invocation identifier, tool name, and input values. In the Anthropic API, the stop_reason value is set to tool_use to indicate that the response was stopped due to a tool call. Nothing has actually been done at this point. All the model did was write a request: “Call this tool with these inputs.”

markers.label: app runs
markers.title: Execution is up to the app code
markers.body: The app code that receives the request takes the input and executes the actual function, API, or command. Since it is the app that runs, it can be inspected, approved, and blocked right before execution. This is why hooks, permission settings, and sandboxes are placed on the app side and not on the model. Exceptions include tools that are run on your behalf by the provider's servers, such as web searches, in which case the app reads the final answer without passing the results.

markers.label: revert result
markers.title: The result is attached to the dialog and returns to the model
markers.body: The app pairs the results of the execution with the call identifier and attaches it to the message of the next request, sending it back to the model. The model reads these results and decides whether to respond with text or request another tool. One round trip of request, execution, and result delivery constitutes one turn of the agent loop. This round trip is repeated until the model produces a response without a tool call.

screens.outro: Let's summarize this repetitive round-trip structure as an agent loop.

ext.title: How tool use works (Claude Platform Docs)

screens.title: Workflows, agents, and agent loops
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and follow step by step the differences between the two structures and how the agent loop goes around.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the agent loop as a circular arrow.
labels: 1 Get prompts, system prompts, tool definitions, and conversation history
2 The model decides to bet on text or tool calls
3 Revert results after running the tool
4 Final result (text, token usage, cost, session ID)

steps.title: Workflow and Agents
steps.body: **Workflow** is a system in which LLM and tools are intertwined into predetermined code paths. **Agent** is a system where LLM dynamically directs the use of procedures and tools. The difference is whether the entity that determines the path is code or a model. Together they are called agentic systems.

steps.title: 1. Receive a prompt
steps.body: The loop starts with the model receiving prompts along with system prompts, tool definitions, and conversation history. The tool definition is a list of what the model can do, and the conversation history contains the results so far.

steps.title: 2. Judge and respond
steps.body: The model looks at the current state and decides how to proceed. You can respond by text, request more than one tool call, or a combination of both. All the model does here is make the call request. It's the next level of app code that actually executes the request.

steps.title: 3. The app runs the tool
steps.body: The harness, or app code that loops outside the model, executes the requested tools and collects the results. The results are returned to the model for further judgment. You can also hook at this point to intercept, modify, or prevent tool calls before they are executed. **Hooks** are custom scripts that the harness runs at set points in the loop. Since it is code, not a request in sentences, it will always behave the same under the same conditions, regardless of whether the model is trying to follow it.

steps.title: 4. Repeat
steps.body: Steps 2 and 3 complete one turn. One round trip is one turn, and we repeat until the model produces a response with no tool calls. Simple questions can be completed in one or two turns, but complex tasks can require dozens of tool calls.

steps.title: 5. Return the result
steps.body: The loop stops when there is a final response without a tool call. The final result is accompanied by result text, token usage, cost, and session ID. What separates an agent from a workflow is that the model looks at each result and changes its approach.

screens.outro: Let's take a look at what is passed to the model each time the loop completes the loop, and why the input continues to grow.

screens.title: Model calls are stateless: context window and tokens
screens.lead: Select and expand each item to see what is passed to the model each time the loop completes. You can expand multiple items at the same time.

items.title: Model calls don't remember previous calls
items.body: Model API calls are stateless. The model stores the contents of the previous call somewhere and does not carry over. So, at each turn, the agent loop sends back all system prompts, tool definitions, history of the conversation so far, and tool results. The reason the agent appears to remember what happened is because the app stitches together the records each time.

items.title: Context Window and Tokens
items.body: The model processes input not as letters, but as tokens, or small pieces of a word. The context window is the limit on the amount of tokens the model can handle in one call. Most model APIs charge based on the number of tokens processed. As records accumulate, the input token becomes larger, increasing both cost and delay. Once the limit is reached, the same conversation cannot continue.

items.title: What happens when it gets longer
items.body: Just because you're within the limit doesn't mean you use all information equally well. Liu et al.'s (2023, TACL 2024) study reported that performance is best when relevant information is at the beginning or end of the input and drops significantly when it is in the middle, and the same trend was seen in models built to handle long inputs. Therefore, agents with long records face a burden not only in terms of cost but also in terms of accuracy.

items.title: Prompt Caching
items.body: Since the previous parts such as tool definitions, system prompts, and previous records are repeated each turn, there is a function to reduce processing time and cost by reusing the previous parts that have already been processed. Anthropic's prompt caching reads from the cache when the tool, system prompt, and message sequence preceding it is the same as the previous request, and the read rate is lower than the normal input rate. However, caching does not change the content created, nor does it change the structure itself, which increases calls and records longer by the number of judgments.

screens.outro: Now, let’s compare ReAct, which established this loop in theory, with the planned structure.

ext.title: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (TACL, 2024)

screens.title: Differences between planned agents and ReAct
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how both methods work and what their benefits and limitations are.

tabs.label: ReAct
tabs.body: The paper "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models" (ICLR 2023) published in 2022 by Yao et al. proposed a method to alternately generate reasoning traces and actions. Inferences allow you to create and update plans and handle exceptions, while actions allow you to retrieve information from external sources such as the Wiki API. This reduces the hallucinations and error propagation common in inference-only approaches, and leaves a human-readable solution process. The key is to use the results obtained from the environment as the basis for each step to judge progress.

tabs.label: Limitations of ReAct
tabs.body: A ReAct-like agent calls the model at every step and chooses the next action. It's effective for simple tasks. However, each subtask requires a large model call, and because you only plan one thing at a time, your overall judgment is poor. Tasks with more steps increase the number of calls and cost.

tabs.label: planning type
tabs.body: A plan-and-execute agent first has a large model plan the entire steps. Each subtask is then taken over by a lighter or domain-specific model, or performed without a model call. If the plan goes wrong, the plan is corrected through the re-planning stage. That is, large models are only used for planning, replanning, and final responses. Studies in the series that divide planning and execution include Plan-and-Solve Prompting (2023) and ReWOO (2023). Plan-and-Solve attempted to reduce errors caused by missing steps by having the model first create a plan divided into subtasks and perform them in order. ReWOO proposed a direction that would reduce repeated prompts each time waiting for a tool response by decoupling reasoning from external observations. The planning description in this screen refers to this plan-execution separation structure.

tabs.label: Three benefits
tabs.body: First, it's fast. Because you don't call a big model for every action. Second, it's cheap. This is because large models are only used for planning, re-planning and final response. Third, performance may increase. This is because it forces the planner to think explicitly about all the necessary steps, breaking them down into sub-problems and focusing on each one.

tabs.label: Which one should I choose?
tabs.body: If the number of steps is small and you need to change direction immediately after seeing the results at each step, the ReAct formula is simple and suitable. For tasks with many steps and where the entire structure can be drawn first, planning reduces the number of calls and costs. When choosing a planning type, you must design a replanning step to go back to if the plan goes wrong.

screens.outro: Now let's look at when to avoid using agents and the costs of autonomy.

ext.title: Yao et al., ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models (ICLR 2023)
Xu et al., ReWOO: Decoupling Reasoning from Observations for Efficient Augmented Language Models (2023)

screens.title: When not to use agents and the costs of autonomy
screens.lead: Move the slider to change how much you can pre-write your task's path. The explanation changes depending on the severity and how the appropriate structure and costs vary.

data.controlLabel: The extent to which the route can be written in advance

stops.body: A single LLM call followed by a search and an example in context is usually sufficient. In this case, the best answer is not to create an agent system. Because agent systems trade off delays and costs for better performance, they start with the simplest solution and increase complexity only when necessary. An FAQ bot that answers a single question is an example of this segment.

When tasks have well-defined procedures, workflows provide predictability and consistency. Same inputs take the same path, making testing and debugging easier and costs more predictable. This includes your order confirmation email. If you use an agent in this area, your costs will only increase and you will gain nothing.

stops.value: Only part of it can be written down
stops.body: The broad framework is set, but judgment is required at some stages. In this case, we consider a workflow that places LLM calls only where needed, within a fixed path. Autonomy is left only to the point where the model's judgment benefits. For example, a configuration where only the email text is refined to suit the situation and the rest is processed with code.

The agent is an open problem in which the number of steps cannot be known in advance and a fixed path cannot be established. This is an environment where flexibility and model-driven judgment are needed at scale, and where there is some level of trust in the model's judgment. Fixing login failure bugs is an example of this section.

Autonomy means increased costs and the potential for errors to accumulate. So you need stopping conditions like sufficient testing in a sandbox, guardrails, and maximum number of iterations. Frameworks make it easy to get started, but they can obscure prompts and responses, making debugging difficult, so you need to understand their internal workings before using them. Check the numbers on the following screen to see why errors are accumulating.

screens.outro: Let’s check in numbers how errors accumulate among the costs of autonomy.

screens.title: How Errors Accumulate: Multiplication of Success Rates for Each Step
screens.lead: Read the short calculation code to see how the overall probability of success changes as the steps increase. The commentary on the right explains the meaning of each line range. The numbers are assumptions to show the structure.

data.code:
#Assumption: Each step independently has a 95% chance of success
step_success = 0.95

for steps in (1, 5, 10, 20, 50):
    all_ok = step_success ** steps
    print(f"Probability of consecutive success in {steps:>2} steps: {all_ok:.1%}")

#execution result
#Stage 1 consecutive success probability: 95.0%
#Success probability for 5 consecutive steps: 77.4%
#Success probability for 10 consecutive steps: 59.9%
#Success probability for 20 consecutive stages: 35.8%
#Success probability for 50 consecutive stages: 7.7%

notes.note: 95% is an assumption made for illustration purposes. In reality, the agent's success rate at each stage varies depending on the task and tool, and the stages are not completely independent of each other. What this code is trying to show is the multiplication structure, not the specific numbers.

For something that requires multiple steps to all succeed, the overall probability of success is the product of the probabilities of the steps. Even though each step seems high, the product quickly decreases as the number of steps increases.

If 95% steps are followed 20 times, the overall probability of success is approximately 36%. In fact, it may be worse than multiplication. This is because errors in the previous step become input to the next step and spread, and the model makes the next decision based on the incorrect results.

Therefore, stopping conditions such as the maximum number of iterations, verification to check the results at each step, and sandbox testing are required. A study measuring the consistency of repeated trials of agents (τ-bench, 2024) also reported that success is inconsistent when solving the same task multiple times.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the concepts, let's solve the problem in the first scene through explanation.

ext.title: Yao et al., tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains (2024)

screens.title: Explanation 1: How costs increase in fixed-process operations
screens.lead: Your instructor will explain step-by-step why automating order confirmation emails increases your costs. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: The original flow is three steps of code:
steps.body: The fixed flow was three steps of code: order tracking, stock confirmation, and template email. If you need an LLM, all it takes is one call to polish your email copy. A structure with fewer calls and more predictable results. This structure makes it easy to calculate the cost per case.

steps.title: Switching to Agent will resend everything every turn.
steps.body: When implemented as an agent, the model receives system prompts, tool definitions, and history so far as input at each turn. Then, it looks at the input and decides the next action. As records accumulate, the input each turn also increases.

steps.title: Tokens are accumulated according to the number of turns.
steps.body: Model calls are stateless, so they resend the entire input for each decision. As the number of turns increases, the recording becomes longer, increasing the cumulative token usage, and since each turn is executed one after another, response time also increases. Although prompt caching lowers the processing cost of the repeated front part, the structure of calls increasing and input lengthening according to the number of decisions remains the same. If the three stages go through three or more model judgments, a corresponding fee is added.

steps.title: Even though the input is the same, the results and costs fluctuate.
steps.body: If the model sometimes changes the order or makes unnecessary queries, the results and costs will be different even with the same input. This reduces predictability, making testing and debugging difficult. Even if you only send one email, there are situations where the cost varies for each call.

steps.title: There is no benefit in judging
steps.body: Since the procedure is always the same, there is no benefit generated by the model's judgment. Even though you don't have to use the agent's advantage of flexibility, you still pay the agent's costs. What the agent can provide in this job is flexibility, but you are paying for flexibility that you don't need.

screens.outro: Let’s compare how the same task changes if you change it to a workflow.

data.notes: The prescription is to have three fixed steps in code and only place one LLM call somewhere like phrase generation. However, if this procedure has many branching exceptions at each step and is difficult to list in advance, there is a reason to revert to the agent. The criterion is not the name of the tool, but whether the path can be pre-written. The first four rows of the table show the differences in cost structure, and the last two rows show maintenance and eligible tasks.

screens.outro: Let's look at the opposite example: the tasks and selection criteria for which the agent is suited.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Counterexamples and selection criteria where the agent is correct
screens.lead: This time, we will solve the tasks for which agents are suited. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: case
steps.body: A request came in to “fix the login failure bug.” You don't know in advance how many files you need to look at or what needs to be fixed. The cause may be in the configuration file or the authentication logic. The request is one line, but the solution path is open.

steps.title: Why Agent
steps.body: The agent is correct because we cannot predict the number of steps required and cannot pin down a fixed route. Pre-writing the path in code would require listing all possible branches, which is not possible for this task.

steps.title: What agents do
steps.body: The agent reads files, modifies them, and runs tests. Then, look at the results returned by the tool and change your approach. If a test fails, the role of the agent loop is to decide the next action according to the situation, such as turning to another file. The result of each tool call becomes the basis for the next action.

steps.title: Three selection criteria
steps.body: Ask three questions in order. First, is it resolved with a single call? Second, is it possible to write down the route in advance? Third, is flexibility needed to bear the cost and error accumulation?

steps.title: Stop at the simplest structure
steps.body: Ask the questions in order, stopping at the simplest structure that results in a “yes.” If it resolves to a single call, that's it, if you can write down the path, it's a workflow, and only by the third time do you select an agent. When choosing an agent, also prepare stopping conditions such as sandbox testing and maximum number of iterations. Judging by this order will help you avoid choosing a structure that is more complicated than necessary.

screens.outro: Now, let's organize the concepts of this lesson into a map.

screens.title: Concept map revisited
screens.lead: Select and expand each concept to see how it connects to the problem in the first scene.

items.title: agent loop
items.body: Iterate through the model's judgment, running the tool, and observing the results until a response is obtained that does not require a tool call. One lap is one turn, and the number of turns directly affects the cost.

items.title: ReAct
items.body: They alternate between reasoning and action, updating their plans with information from the environment. For simple tasks, this method is simple and effective.

items.title: planning agent
items.body: The big model builds the overall plan first and performs subtasks lightly. If the plan goes wrong, you have to re-plan.

items.title: When not to use it
items.body: If a single call or fixed workflow is sufficient, no agent is used. Order confirmation emails are a prime example.

items.title: cost of autonomy
items.body: Autonomy is traded for costs, delays, and accumulated errors. Manage risk with outage conditions and testing.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the judgment criteria one more time.

screens.title: Questions to ask before designing automation
screens.lead: The content of this class is organized into questions that can be used immediately at work. Read it slowly.

paragraphs: When designing new automation, the first question to ask is not “Should I use an agent?” but “Can I write down the path for this task in advance?” If you can write it down, your workflow will be cheaper and more predictable. If it resolves to a single call, that's the simplest answer.

We consider structures in which the model determines its own procedures only in open problems where the path cannot be written down. This comes at the cost of autonomy, so we design stopping conditions, sandbox testing, and maximum number of iterations together.
Just asking these two questions first in business meetings can significantly reduce the chances of choosing the wrong structure.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: For workflows, the code determines the path, and for agents, the model determines the path. Look at which one is right for the job, not which one is more advanced.

glossary.def: It is a cycle of repeating the model's judgment, executing the tool, and observing the results until a response is obtained that does not require a tool call.
It alternates between inferences and actions and updates the plan with external information.
The structure is to first make an overall plan, execute subtasks, and re-plan if necessary.
It is a system in which LLM and tools are intertwined with a predetermined code path.
It is one round trip in the agent loop, consisting of a tool call and reflection of the result.
The model makes a structured request containing the tool name and input values, and then the app code actually executes it and returns the results to the conversation.

misconceptions.myth: Agents are always a more advanced structure than workflows.
misconceptions.fact: For tasks where the route can be written down in advance, the workflow is cheaper and more predictable. A more complex structure is not better; choose the simplest structure that suits the task.

misconceptions.myth: Once you use a tool, you become an agent.
misconceptions.fact: The key is that the model sets its own procedures and repeats them. Invoking tools within a path determined by code is a workflow.
If the plan goes wrong, replanning is necessary, and for simple tasks, ReAct is simpler. Choose between the two methods depending on the nature of the task.

misconceptions.myth: The model runs the tool directly.
misconceptions.fact: The model is only involved in making the call request, and execution is left to the app code or provider server. Since the execution entity is an app, inspection, approval, and blocking can be included before execution.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: For workflows, the code determines the path, and for agents, the model determines the path.
The agent loop iterates through judgment, execution of tools, and observation of results until a final response is reached.
ReAct mixes reasoning and action, while Planning makes the overall plan first, reducing calls and costs.
Fixed procedure tasks are cheaper and more predictable in workflows or single calls.
The cost of autonomy is worth paying only in open problems where the path cannot be written down in advance.
